name: Imagine Worldwide: tablet-based literacy and numeracy (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults: BEFIT in Malawi's government schools (92.6%) and the Dzaleka camp in Malawi; the other countries by the children Imagine served there in 2024 (Annual Report p. 12).
summary: Imagine Worldwide funds and coordinates tablet-based, child-directed literacy and numeracy software (onebillion's onecourse) in government primary schools, chiefly Malawi's national BEFIT roll-out, with pilots in Sierra Leone and five other African countries; in 2024 it served about 435,000 children. Counting a year of tablet learning per child against 2024's cost (equipment spread over its life), and the learning gain as later earnings, the model gives about 2.3 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars. The biggest uncertainties are how much of a learning gain lasts into adult earnings and how well the trials' effects hold at national scale; the countries outside Malawi, with no trial of the programme as delivered there, are discounted for missing data.

rows.label: Cost of a tablet with headphones and case
rows.explainer: Judgment $80 ($50-150): a rugged low-cost Android tablet bought in bulk with headphones and a case. Anchor: Imagine's own all-in figure of under $7 a child a year with equipment spread over its life and five children per tablet (BEFIT overview p. 3) leaves a few dollars a child a year for the tablet, which fits $50-100 over four to five years; the high end allows for replacements, accessories and shipping.

rows.label: Cost of a school's solar system with charging and storage cabinets
rows.explainer: Judgment $6,000 ($3,000-12,000): panels, batteries and charge controllers sized to charge a school's tablets daily, plus the lockable charging and storage cages local fabricators build (BEFIT overview p. 3). Off-grid school systems of a few kilowatts cost in this range in eastern and southern Africa.

rows.label: Years a tablet lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 4 years (3-6): used by about five children a day; the Year 2 report names broken headphones, cords and slow repairs as the main problem (pp. 17-18, 27), and Imagine is building a repair network to extend tablets' life (Annual Report p. 24).

rows.label: Years a solar system lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 15 years (10-20): Imagine expects 20+ years of power from the panels (BEFIT overview p. 2); batteries are replaced sooner.

rows.label: Equipment bought in 2024 (in the year's cash spending)
rows.explainer: Tablets and solar systems added in 2024, at their unit costs: taken out of the year's spending, because they serve children for years.

rows.label: Yearly cost of all equipment in service in 2024, spread over its life
rows.formula: tablets_in_service_2024 * tablet_unit_cost / tablet_life_years + solar_systems_2024 * solar_unit_cost / solar_life_years
rows.explainer: The year's share of every tablet and solar system in use in 2024, those bought in 2023 included: what 2024's children used up.

rows.label: Programme cost of 2024, equipment counted at its yearly cost
rows.explainer: The year's programme spending with equipment bought replaced by the yearly cost of the equipment in use, so the cost matches the children served in the same year (one year's flow against one year's cost). Everything else (Imagine Malawi's coordination, local partners' training and monitoring, research, the new country teams) counts as spent in the year, including the training for schools launched in September 2024 that serves them in later years too; no published figure splits it out, so the cost is slightly high on this count.

rows.label: Learning gain per child-year of the combined literacy and numeracy software (SD, average of the two)

source.title: Imagine Worldwide, 'Summary of Research on onebillion's Learning Software' (September 2023), Table 2
source.quote: Effect size for overall math (EGMA average % correct) 0.07(5) 0.54** 0.26* 0.02(5) 0.44***

rows.explainer: Imagine's five-month randomised trial in Tanzanian government schools gave the combined literacy-and-maths software, as BEFIT now does, for 40 minutes a day after school (20 hours a subject): intent-to-treat effects of 0.34 SD on literacy and 0.26 SD on maths, average 0.30. Being after school, it adds time rather than replacing lessons; BEFIT's sessions replace other lessons in the school day, as in Imagine's Malawi trials, which are net of the lessons displaced but needed more time on one subject for similar effects (0.34 literacy and 0.07 maths after 56 hours, 0.37 literacy and 0.54 maths after 101 hours). BEFIT children averaged 36 hours a year across both subjects. 0.25 (0.12-0.40): below the Tanzanian trial for school-day delivery at that dose. Intent-to-treat effects include children who missed sessions.

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per SD of learning that lasts into working life
rows.explainer: Judgment 20% (10-40%), the same figure as charityevals' other education branches in low- and middle-income countries (Save the Children, the International Rescue Committee, the Norwegian Refugee Council, Jesuit Refugee Service, USA for UNHCR), to be read from a shared fact once one exists: an SD of adult numeracy goes with 18% higher wages across PIAAC countries (Hanushek, Schwerdt, Wiederhold and Woessmann, NBER Working Paper 19762, https://www.nber.org/papers/w19762), and a year of schooling raises earnings about 9% while adding well under one SD of learning in poor countries.

rows.label: Share of the learning gain still there in adult life
rows.explainer: Judgment 40% (20-80%), the same figure as charityevals' other education branches, to be read from a shared fact once one exists: test-score effects of education programmes fade in the years after them (Bailey, Duncan, Odgers and Yu 2017, 'initially promising but then quickly disappearing impacts', https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5779101/).

rows.label: Years from the tablet year to adult earnings
rows.explainer: Judgment 10 years (7-13): children in Standards 1-4 are about 6 to 12 (many older than their grade), and start earning in their late teens.

rows.label: Years the earnings gain lasts
rows.explainer: The shared figure for long-term income gains (@givewell_shared.long_term_benefit_years).

rows.label: Household members who share the earnings gain
rows.explainer: The shared figure (@givewell_shared.resource_sharing_multiplier), as in every model of later-life income.

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) per child for a year of tablet learning, discounted to today
rows.formula: ln(1 + rct_learning_gain_sd * edu_earnings_per_sd * edu_persistence) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - years_until_work) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: ln(1 + learning gain × earnings per SD × share lasting) in each working year, discounted to today from when work starts, shared in the household. A proportional gain, so the level of consumption cancels.

rows.label: Consumption per person in Malawi, survey mean (2021 PPP dollars a year, for reading)
rows.explainer: For reading only: the earnings gain is a share of the children's later consumption, so ln(1 + gain) doesn't depend on its level.

rows.label: Benefits to other people, as a share of the children's benefits
rows.explainer: Judgment 5% (0-20%): parents report children teaching them reading, maths and the use of technology (the Year 2 survey asked; Annual Report p. 18 quotes a father), and more literate classmates may help others. No measurement, so small and wide.

rows.label: Mortality benefits as a share of consumption benefits
rows.explainer: 0: no trial of tablet learning measures deaths; the longer-run health benefits of literacy (including for the children's own future children) are counted in unmodelled_benefits_adj instead.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.7 (0.4-0.9): how far to trust the trials themselves; how much survives at scale is mw_implementation_adj. The trials are consistent (nine randomised trials of the software, all positive) but each is small (one or two schools, children randomised within them), run and reported by Imagine itself, and the charity's own summary is where the effects are collected, so some selection and small-sample inflation is likely. Above charityevals' Save the Children education branch (0.6), whose effect is a literature median for programmes unlike its own. The independent evaluations of BEFIT at scale (a World Bank comparison of 40 schools with 40 matched ones, and a University of Chicago trial in 348 schools, Year 2 report p. 7) aren't published yet.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%): the trial effects are already net of children taught as usual. What isn't is whether Malawi's government and other funders would have rolled out tablet learning without Imagine; 292 of the 460 Year 2 schools had used an earlier version of the software under VSO's Unlocking Talent programme (Year 2 report p. 8), which had ended, and no other funder had a national plan.

rows.label: Imagine's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 84% (70-95%): Imagine pays for the tablets, solar power, training and coordination, but government teachers run the sessions in school time (90-175 minutes a week a class, Year 2 report p. 6), the Ministry's BEFIT unit manages the roll-out, and onebillion gives the software royalty-free (BEFIT overview p. 3) after developing it with other funding. About 10,000 teachers trained, giving perhaps a tenth of their time at Malawi's teacher pay, is a few per cent of the cost; onebillion's development and the Ministry's staff a few per cent more. Outside Malawi, partners pay part of the work (the USDA McGovern-Dole programme with Counterpart and Catholic Relief Services in Senegal and Burkina Faso, Rising Academy in Liberia and Ghana; Annual Report p. 12), about one per cent of the whole.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: Imagine's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Judgment 1 (0.85-1.2). Above 1: philanthropy matched 1:1 brought in $15.2 million of Global Partnership for Education money for Malawi (Annual Report p. 9), and the government commits to pay running costs later. Below 1: that money would otherwise fund other education in Malawi. No net direction is evident.

rows.label: Malawi: learning at scale against the trial, per child-year
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (40-100%). BEFIT children averaged 36 hours on the tablets in 2024/25, close to the Tanzanian trial's 40 hours, but 32% of schools fell short of the 27-hour target, broken headphones and software glitches disrupted sessions, teachers' motivation varied (Year 2 report pp. 16-18, 27), and a school's second-year gains were smaller than its first (p. 26), while children stay four years. The report's before-and-after gains (7 points of literacy, 10 of numeracy) have no control group, so they are a check, not the effect.

rows.label: Other countries: learning against the trial, per child-year
rows.explainer: Judgment 55% (25-90%): mostly pilots, two-thirds in Sierra Leone, where the software is in English, a language many children don't speak at home, and reading gains fell short of Imagine's target (Annual Report p. 20); its trial in Dzaleka camp, also in English, found almost no maths gain (0.02 SD, Research Summary Table 2). Below Malawi's 70%.

rows.label: Malawi: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: 1, measured: Imagine's own count of the children in BEFIT schools meets effects from its own randomised trials of the same software in government schools: the combined-software trial in Tanzania gives the effect, and its trials in Chichewa in Malawian government schools during the school day, BEFIT's own setting, bound it.

rows.label: Other countries: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step: in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ghana, Senegal and Burkina Faso (94% of these children) no controlled trial measures the programme as delivered there (English or French software, partners' delivery); the effect is the Tanzanian trial's. Dzaleka camp (3,653) had a trial, but of an English maths-only version that found almost no effect, unlike the programme now run there by refugee-led partners; Tanzania's 650 are in schools handed to local control. Both stay in this branch, too few to split out.

rows.label: Malawi: all adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * leverage_funging_adj * mw_implementation_adj * mw_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Other countries: all adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * leverage_funging_adj * oth_implementation_adj * oth_missing_data_adj

Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Judgment +12% (-3% to +30%): literacy's benefits beyond earnings, such as health knowledge, civic life and better health for the children's own future children (+8%); solar power left in about 900 schools for lighting and other uses, and digital skills for teachers (98% report enjoying teaching more, Year 2 report p. 30) (+5%); against teachers' extra burden (42% report more, p. 30) and electronic waste (-1%). Attendance gains reported by stakeholders are not counted: they are perceptions, not measured.
